050.exp: Germany's economic system is the "soziale Marktwirtschaft" (social market economy). This model was developed by Ludwig Erhard after WWII and combines free market principles with social welfare policies. Businesses operate freely and compete in the market, but the state intervenes to provide social security, prevent monopolies, and ensure fair working conditions. The GDR (East Germany) had a "Planwirtschaft" (planned economy), where the state controlled all economic activity.

051.q: It is NOT part of a democratic rule-of-law state that …
opts: people can express criticism of the government.
citizens are allowed to participate in peaceful demonstrations.
people are arrested without cause by a private police force.
someone commits a crime and is therefore arrested.
051.exp: In a democratic Rechtsstaat, only the state police can arrest people, and only with legal justification. A "private police" arresting people without reason would be illegal and undemocratic. Criticizing the government, peaceful demonstrations, and lawful arrests for crimes are all normal parts of a democratic society.

052.q: What does "popular sovereignty" mean? All state authority emanates from the …
052.exp: "Volkssouveränität" (popular sovereignty) is established in Article 20 of the Basic Law: "Alle Staatsgewalt geht vom Volke aus" — "All state authority emanates from the people." This means the people are the ultimate source of political power. They exercise this power through elections and votes. The Bundestag represents the people, but the power originates from the citizens themselves.

053.q: What does "Rechtsstaat" (rule of law) mean in Germany?
opts: The state must abide by the laws.
053.exp: "Rechtsstaat" literally translates to "law state" or "state of law." It means the state and all its institutions are bound by law — the government cannot act arbitrarily but must follow legal rules. This is different from "the state is right" (a common misunderstanding) or "only right-wing parties" (a play on the word "Recht" which can mean both "law/right" and "right-wing").

054.q: Which is NOT a branch of state power in Germany?
054.exp: Germany's state power is divided into three branches: Legislative (law-making), Executive (Exekutive, law-enforcing), and Judiciary (Judikative, law-interpreting). "Direktive" is not a real branch of government — it is the trick answer.

opts: the seat of the Bundestag in Berlin
the Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe
055.exp: The picture shows the Reichstag building in Berlin, which houses the German Bundestag (federal parliament) — recognizable by its glass dome.

056.q: Which office belongs to municipal administration in Germany?
056.exp: The Ordnungsamt (public order office) is a municipal authority responsible for local public order and safety. The Pfarramt is religious, the Finanzamt is a state tax office, and the Auswärtiges Amt is the federal foreign ministry — none are municipal.

057.q: Who is usually elected President of the German Bundestag?
opts: the Minister-President of the largest federal state
a member of the strongest parliamentary group
057.exp: By convention, the President of the Bundestag is a member of the strongest parliamentary group (Fraktion), not necessarily the oldest MP or a former Chancellor.

058.q: Who appoints the ministers of the federal government in Germany?
opts: the President of the Federal Constitutional Court
058.exp: The Federal President formally appoints and dismisses federal ministers, on the proposal of the Chancellor.

059.q: How many years ago did a Jewish community first exist on the territory of present-day Germany?
059.exp: Jewish communities have existed on German territory for about 1,700 years, with documented evidence dating to Roman-era Cologne in 321 CE — among the oldest Jewish settlements in Europe north of the Alps.

060.q: In Germany, the Bundestag and Bundesrat belong to the …
060.exp: The Bundestag and Bundesrat are both legislative bodies (Legislative) — they make laws, unlike the executive (government) or judiciary (courts).

opts: The king/queen rules over the people.
The Federal Constitutional Court stands above the constitution.
Interest groups exercise sovereignty together with the government.
State power originates from the people.
061.exp: Popular sovereignty, enshrined in Article 20 of the Basic Law, means all state authority is derived from the people, exercised through elections and referenda.

062.q: When the parliament of a German federal state is elected, this is called …
062.exp: Electing a state parliament (Landtag) is called a Landtagswahl, distinct from municipal, European, or federal elections.

063.q: What does NOT belong to the executive branch in Germany?
063.exp: Courts belong to the judiciary (Judikative), not the executive. Police, tax offices, and ministries are all part of the executive branch.

064.q: Today, the Federal Republic of Germany is organized into …
opts: an eastern state and a western state.
064.exp: Germany's administrative structure has three levels: the federal government (Bund), the 16 states (Länder), and local municipalities (Kommunen).

065.q: It is NOT a task of the German Bundestag to …
065.exp: Forming the cabinet is the Chancellor's job, not the Bundestag's. The Bundestag drafts laws, elects the Chancellor, and controls the government.

066.q: Which cities have the largest Jewish communities in Germany?
066.exp: Berlin and Munich have Germany's largest Jewish communities today, reflecting post-reunification and post-Soviet immigration patterns.

067.q: What is primarily a task of the federal states in Germany?
067.exp: Education policy (Schulpolitik) is primarily a state responsibility in Germany, unlike defense, foreign affairs, and much of economic policy, which are federal matters.

068.q: Why does the state control the school system in Germany?
opts: because there are only state schools in Germany
because all students must have a school qualification
because there are different schools in the federal states
because it is the state's responsibility under the Basic Law
068.exp: State oversight of schools (Schulaufsicht) is a constitutional duty under the Basic Law, ensuring educational quality and standards nationwide.

069.q: Germany has a three-tier administrative structure. What is the lowest political level called?
069.exp: The Gemeinden (municipalities) form the lowest administrative and political level in Germany's three-tier structure of Bund, Länder, and Gemeinden.

070.q: In 1974, German President Gustav Heinemann hands Helmut Schmidt his certificate of appointment as Federal Chancellor. What is one of the duties of the German Federal President?
opts: He/she runs the day-to-day business of government.
He/she proposes the Chancellor for election.
070.exp: The Federal President proposes a candidate for Chancellor to the Bundestag for election, and formally appoints the Chancellor and ministers — but does not run the government or select ministers personally.

071.q: Where is the German Federal Chancellor most often located? He/she is most often …
opts: in Bonn, because the Chancellery and Bundestag are located there.
in Berlin, because the Chancellery and Bundestag are located there.
at Schloss Meseberg, the government's guest house, to receive state guests.
at Schloss Bellevue, the President's official residence, to receive state guests.
071.exp: Since the government moved from Bonn to Berlin in 1999, the Chancellor is most often in Berlin, home to both the Chancellery and the Bundestag.

072.q: What is the name of the current Federal Chancellor of Germany?
072.exp: Friedrich Merz (CDU) has been Federal Chancellor since 2025. Note: this is a current-affairs question the real test updates periodically — always verify the current officeholder before the exam.

073.q: The two largest parliamentary groups in the German Bundestag are currently called …
073.exp: Following the 2025 federal election, CDU/CSU and AfD are the two largest parliamentary groups. Note: this is a current-affairs question — verify before the exam, as party standings change with each election.

074.q: What is the parliament for all of Germany called?
074.exp: The Bundestag is Germany's national parliament. The Bundesversammlung only convenes to elect the President, the Volkskammer was the former East German parliament, and the Bundesgerichtshof is a court.

075.q: What is the name of Germany's current head of state?
075.exp: Frank-Walter Steinmeier is Germany's Federal President (head of state). Note: this is a current-affairs question — verify the current officeholder before the exam.

076.q: What does the abbreviation CDU stand for in Germany?
076.exp: CDU stands for Christlich Demokratische Union (Christian Democratic Union), one of Germany's major political parties.

077.exp: The Bundeswehr is Germany's armed forces (the military), not the police, a port, or a citizens' group.

078.q: What does the abbreviation SPD stand for?
078.exp: SPD stands for Sozialdemokratische Partei Deutschlands (Social Democratic Party of Germany), one of Germany's oldest and largest parties.

079.q: What does the abbreviation FDP stand for in Germany?
079.exp: FDP stands for Freie Demokratische Partei (Free Democratic Party), a liberal party in Germany.

080.q: Which court in Germany is responsible for interpreting the Basic Law?
080.exp: The Bundesverfassungsgericht (Federal Constitutional Court), located in Karlsruhe, is responsible for interpreting the Basic Law and reviewing the constitutionality of laws.

081.q: Who elects the Federal Chancellor in Germany?
081.exp: The Bundestag elects the Federal Chancellor, on the proposal of the Federal President — not the people directly, the Bundesrat, or the Bundesversammlung (which only elects the President).

082.q: Who leads the German federal cabinet?
082.exp: The Federal Chancellor leads the federal cabinet and determines the general policy guidelines (Richtlinienkompetenz).

083.q: Who elects the German Federal Chancellor?
083.exp: The Bundestag elects the Federal Chancellor — Germans do not vote for the Chancellor directly.

084.q: What is the main task of the German Federal President? He/she …
084.exp: The Federal President's main role is representative (a largely ceremonial head of state) — the Chancellor governs, and the Bundestag drafts laws.

085.q: Who makes up the German Bundesrat?
opts: the ministers of the federal government
government representatives of the federal states
085.exp: The Bundesrat consists of representatives of the state governments (Länder), representing regional interests in federal legislation.

086.q: Who elects the Federal President in Germany?
086.exp: The Bundesversammlung (Federal Convention) — a special body of Bundestag members and state delegates — elects the Federal President every five years.

087.q: Who is the head of state of the Federal Republic of Germany?
087.exp: The Federal President is Germany's head of state, a largely ceremonial role, distinct from the Chancellor who heads the government.

088.q: The parliamentary opposition in the German Bundestag …
opts: decides who becomes a federal minister.
determines who sits in the Bundesrat.
proposes the heads of government of the states.
088.exp: The parliamentary opposition's key role is to control and scrutinize the government — it does not appoint ministers or determine Bundesrat/state leadership.

089.q: What is the association of a party's members of parliament called in Germany?
089.exp: A Fraktion is the parliamentary group formed by members of the same party (or allied parties) in the Bundestag.

090.q: The German federal states participate in federal legislation through …
090.exp: The Bundesrat is the chamber through which the states participate in federal lawmaking, giving them a voice in national legislation.

091.q: In Germany, a change of government in a federal state can affect federal politics. Governing becomes …
opts: harder, if this changes the majority in the Bundestag.
easier, if new parties enter the Bundesrat.
harder, if this changes the majority in the Bundesrat.
easier, if it is a wealthy federal state.
091.exp: Since state governments sit in the Bundesrat, a shift in a state election can change the Bundesrat majority, making federal governing harder if the opposition gains ground there.

092.q: What does the abbreviation CSU stand for in Germany?
092.exp: CSU stands for Christlich Soziale Union (Christian Social Union), the Bavaria-only sister party of the CDU.

093.q: The more "second votes" a party receives in a federal election, the …
opts: more seats the party gets in parliament.
fewer first votes it can have.
more of the party's direct candidates enter parliament.
greater the risk of having to form a coalition.
093.exp: The Zweitstimme (second vote) determines each party's overall share of Bundestag seats — the more second votes, the more total seats.

094.q: From what age can one participate in the election to the German Bundestag?
094.exp: The minimum voting age for federal (Bundestag) elections in Germany is 18.

095.q: What applies to most children in Germany?
095.exp: Compulsory schooling (Schulpflicht) applies to nearly all children in Germany — voting, confidentiality, and religion are not compulsory for children.

096.q: How can someone who denies the Holocaust be punished?
opts: up to 100 hours of community service
not at all; Holocaust denial is permitted
with imprisonment of up to five years or a fine
096.exp: Holocaust denial is a criminal offense in Germany under §130(3) StGB (Volksverhetzung — incitement to hatred). Anyone who publicly denies, downplays, or approves of the Nazi genocide can face up to 5 years in prison or a fine. This law reflects Germany's historical responsibility for the murder of 6 million Jews. Germany takes this very seriously — it is NOT a matter of free speech but a criminal act.

097.q: What does one automatically pay in Germany when permanently employed?
097.exp: Permanently employed workers automatically pay into social insurance (Sozialversicherung) — covering health, pension, unemployment, and long-term care.

098.q: When members of the German Bundestag switch parliamentary groups, ...
opts: the government can lose its majority.
they may no longer attend parliamentary sessions.
the Federal President must first give consent.
voters of these members may vote again.
098.exp: If enough MPs switch groups, the governing coalition can lose its parliamentary majority, since coalitions rely on a specific seat count.

099.q: Who pays social insurance contributions in Germany?
099.exp: Social insurance contributions are shared between employers and employees, each paying roughly half.
